title: Arrays, Strings & the Array–Pointer Relationship
relevance: C array/pointer decay, null-terminated strings, and buffer safety are staple SDE/OA topics because they expose how candidates reason about memory, types, and undefined behavior.

phases.goal: Establish what C arrays and strings are as raw contiguous memory with no runtime length or bounds checking.

must_hit.point: An array is a fixed-size, contiguous sequence of elements of the same type.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says identical elements laid out sequentially so any index address is base plus index times element size.

must_hit.point: C does not store an array's length at runtime and does not perform bounds checking; out-of-range access is undefined behavior.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions scores[10] simply reads whatever is at that address—no length metadata, no automatic check.

must_hit.point: A C string is a char array that ends at the first null character '\0' (byte value 0); memory must be at least one byte larger than the visible text for the terminator.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes null termination and that "Hello" needs room for the trailing '\0'.

must_hit.point: Historically an array's size must be known at compile time; indexing is zero-based; uninitialized arrays hold garbage, and partial init like int zeroes[100] = {0} zeroes the rest.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Covers compile-time size, zero-based indexing, garbage vs zero-fill on partial initialization.

probes: What is an array in C, and what does the language store (or not store) about its length at runtime?
How is a string represented in C, and why must its buffer be larger than the visible text?

hints.1: Think about raw contiguous memory, not a list or string object.
hints.2: Contrast fixed contiguous storage and zero-based indexing with the '\0' convention for strings.
hints.3: Say: fixed-size contiguous same-type block; no runtime length/bounds checks; a string is chars ending at '\0' with one extra byte for the terminator.

phases.goal: Explain array-to-pointer decay, the sizeof/& exceptions, function argument decay, string declaration forms, and 2D layout/types.

must_hit.point: Except as operand of sizeof, unary &, or a string literal used to initialize an array, an array expression decays to a pointer to its first element.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States decay to &a[0] in most expressions, with those three exceptions named.

must_hit.point: a[i] is defined as *(a + i); because addition is commutative, i[a] is also valid C.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Equates subscripting with pointer arithmetic and notes the commutative quirk.

must_hit.point: Passing an array to a function decays it; int arr[] is rewritten to int *arr, so the callee gets a copy of the address and loses the array length.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says the parameter is really a pointer and length must be passed separately.

must_hit.point: char s[] = "hello" allocates a stack array and copies the literal (modifiable); char *p = "hello" points at a read-only data-segment literal.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts copied writable array vs pointer into read-only storage.

must_hit.point: A 2D array like int grid[2][3] is stored contiguously in row-major order; grid decays to a pointer to an array (int (*)[3]), which differs from int *p[3] and int **p.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes one strip of six ints and distinguishes pointer-to-array, array-of-pointers, and pointer-to-pointer.

must_hit.point: sizeof(a) on int a[5] yields the full array size (e.g. 20 for 5×4-byte ints), proving an array is not a pointer; sizeof of a decayed pointer is pointer-sized (e.g. 8 on 64-bit).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses the sizeof exception with the file's 20 vs 8 contrast to refute "array is a pointer."

probes: Is an array a pointer? How would you prove your answer with sizeof?
What actually gets passed when you call a function with an array argument?
How does char s[] = "hello" differ from char *p = "hello" in memory?

hints.1: Start from what happens when you write the array's name in an expression.
hints.2: Name the decay exceptions, then what a function parameter int arr[] really is, then string array vs pointer.
hints.3: Decay to &first unless sizeof/&/string-array init; a[i]==*(a+i); callee gets int*; s[] copies writable, *p points read-only; 2D is row-major and decays to int (*)[width].

phases.goal: Compare APIs and representations where the wrong choice causes overflow, UB, or stack failure.

must_hit.point: memcpy assumes non-overlapping regions (overlap is undefined); memmove safely copies even when dest and src overlap.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Chooses memmove whenever overlap is possible; reserves memcpy for proven-disjoint blocks.

must_hit.point: strcpy copies including '\0' but does not know dest size, so an oversized src can overflow; length must be managed by the caller.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Warns that strcpy blindly writes and needs a large enough destination.

must_hit.point: VLAs size the array at runtime on the call stack; a large n (e.g. user input) can blow the stack; C11 made VLAs optional, and in C23 VLA types are mandatory while stack VLA objects remain optional.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links VLA convenience to stack limits and the C11/C23 optional-object status.

must_hit.point: A true 2D contiguous array suits fixed rectangular grids; an array of pointers (int *p[3]) suits distinct rows/strings of different lengths.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Picks contiguous 2D for uniform grid layout vs pointer array when row lengths differ.

probes: When would you use memmove instead of memcpy?
What is the risk of a variable-length array sized from user input?
When is an array of pointers preferable to a true 2D array?

hints.1: Think about overlap, destination capacity, and where the memory lives.
hints.2: Compare memcpy vs memmove, strcpy's ignorance of dest size, VLA-on-stack vs optional status, and contiguous 2D vs pointer rows.
hints.3: memmove if overlap possible; never trust strcpy on unknown dest size; VLAs are stack-limited and optional as objects; use pointer arrays for uneven row lengths.

phases.goal: Apply decay, string conventions, and 2D indexing to concrete interview checks and small algorithms.

must_hit.point: Inside a function, sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0]) fails after decay: sizeof(arr) is pointer size (e.g. 8), so 8/4 yields 2; always pass length separately.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows the broken length formula and the fix void f(int *arr, size_t length).

must_hit.point: char *s = "x"; s[0] = 'Y'; crashes because the literal is in read-only data; use char s[] = "x" to copy onto the stack for modification.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names read-only segment / segfault and the array declaration fix.

must_hit.point: Map 2D (r, c) into a 1D array of WIDTH columns as index r × WIDTH + c.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States skip r full rows of WIDTH, then add c.

must_hit.point: In-place string reverse: walk left and right indices toward the center swapping until they meet, with right starting at len-1 (before '\0'); strlen does not count the terminator.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes two-pointer/index swap loop that leaves '\0' in place.

probes: Why does sizeof-based length calculation fail inside a function that takes int arr[5]?
Why does char *s = "x"; s[0] = 'Y'; crash, and how do you make the string modifiable?
How do you map a 2D coordinate (r, c) into a 1D array of WIDTH columns?

hints.1: Ask what type the parameter really has after the call.
hints.2: Tie decay to the failed sizeof ratio, literals to read-only storage, and 2D to row-major indexing.
hints.3: arr is int* so sizeof gives pointer bytes (e.g. 8/4=2); write via char s[] copy; 1D index is r*WIDTH+c; reverse swaps toward the center before '\0'.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Use memcpy only when source and destination do not overlap; if they might overlap, use memmove, which is defined to copy safely in that case.
The array form allocates and copies a writable buffer (e.g. on the stack); the pointer form points at a read-only string literal in the binary's data segment, so writes through it are invalid.

tradeoffs.topic: True 2D array vs array of pointers
tradeoffs.strong_answer: int grid[2][3] is one contiguous row-major block and decays to int (*)[3]; int *p[3] is an array of pointers useful when rows or strings have different lengths.

tradeoffs.topic: VLA stack objects vs avoiding them
tradeoffs.strong_answer: VLAs are sized at runtime on the call stack and can overflow it for large n; C11 made VLAs optional, and C23 requires VLA types but leaves creating VLA objects on the stack optional.

gotchas.trap: Believing "an array is just a pointer."
gotchas.correction: Arrays and pointers are different types. Decay makes an array evaluate to a pointer in most expressions, but sizeof(a) on int a[5] yields the full array size (e.g. 20), not a pointer size (e.g. 8).

gotchas.trap: Using sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0]) inside a function to get the array length.
gotchas.correction: The parameter decayed to a pointer, so sizeof(arr) is the pointer size; e.g. 8/4 = 2. Always pass the length as a separate argument.

gotchas.trap: Assuming strcpy is safe, or using memcpy when regions may overlap.
gotchas.correction: strcpy does not know dest capacity and can buffer-overflow. memcpy with overlap is undefined; use memmove when overlap is possible.
The literal lives in read-only storage; writes can segfault. Declare char s[] = "literal" so a modifiable copy is made.

gotchas.trap: Using a large runtime VLA from untrusted input.
gotchas.correction: VLAs allocate on the limited call stack and can instantly stack-overflow; treat them as dangerous, and note stack VLA objects are optional in modern C.
